comment: Rewrite plan step 5. Deliberately default-ALLOW with an explicit DENY list, not a reproduction of Docker's own default-DENY allowlist: a hand-rolled allowlist risks silently breaking a legitimate pandas/numpy/openpyxl operation in a way that is hard to diagnose from outside the container, while a default-allow denylist can only ever remove a specific named capability, never accidentally grant one. Every name below is a syscall a CSV/Excel data-transformation process never legitimately needs: process introspection/injection (ptrace, process_vm_*), filesystem-namespace/mount manipulation, kernel-module and kexec loading, raw device/IO-port access, time manipulation, and the whole socket family (redundant with --network none at the namespace level, but seccomp denies it at the syscall level too -- defense in depth, not the only layer). This still runs underneath, not instead of, Docker's own default profile: --security-opt seccomp replaces it wholesale, so anything Docker's default already denies (Docker's default is itself a default-DENY allowlist) is preserved only insofar as it is re-denied here; the plan's four named syscalls (ptrace, mount, unshare, kexec_load) and their close relatives are all listed explicitly below for that reason.

syscalls.comment: namespace-escape primitives specifically (unshare/setns create or join a NEW namespace -- never blocking plain fork/clone, which multiprocessing and pandas/numpy's own worker pools may legitimately use, and which the --pids-limit cgroup ceiling bounds instead)
system clock manipulation -- a data transform reads, never sets, time
NUMA / memory-policy manipulation and handle-based filesystem escapes

the entire socket family: --network none already removes every routable interface, this denies the syscalls outright as well (defense in depth). A CSV/Excel transform never legitimately opens a socket of any kind.
